speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what is the contribution of Total Factor Productivity (TFP) to GDP growth in each of the past 10 years; (b) what has been the growth in TFP in each of the past 10 years; (c) how does Singapore's TFP performance compare to that of other developed countries; and (d) what drivers and restraints of Singapore's recent TFP growth has the Ministry identified.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Between 2008 and 2018, France's TFP rose by 0.3% per annum, while Finland's TFP growth was 0% per annum.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: TFP growth in Germany and in the United States were similar to ours, at about 0.5% per annum.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Initiatives like SkillsFuture to upskill our workers and support lifelong learning would have also contributed to this.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Transforming our economy and raising TFP are long-term efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are making progress, but we must continue to focus on these areas in the years ahead, building on the strong tripartite partnership among the Government, employers and the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first question pertains to the data that was shared.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Parliamentary Question seeks information for each of the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand the Minister of State for Manpower said that the ITMs are launched in different years so it would be more useful to provide data in a certain manner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there is information provided for Singaporeans, Permanent Residents (PRs) and foreigners between the years 2015 and 2018.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Within these years, which ITM is the Minister of State referring to vis-à-vis the numbers of 39,000 Singaporeans, 8,600 PRs and 28,500 foreigners?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, which ITM is the Minister of State referring to?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question is the statistics for Adapt and Grow regarding the 93,000 locals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand "locals" would mean PRs and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can he also share the number of Singaporeans and PRs on Adapt and Grow between these years?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My third question pertains to how information on the ITMs is presented.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The roadmaps are not consistent in terms of jobs for Singaporeans, PRs or foreigners, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Construction ITM, if you go on the respective YouTube channels and you see reference on construction, it is very clear, good jobs for Singaporeans, no two ways about that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: You go to the Retail ITM, they talk about a future-ready workforce and a professional and skilled workforce.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ostensibly, this would mean a whole range, beyond Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Infocomm and Media ITM talks about creating new professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMET) jobs, 13,000 new PMET jobs and it goes on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, every ITM is different and understandably so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But will the Ministry in future, in going forward, present that data very clearly for each ITM, for example, PRs, this many; Singaporeans, this many?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The conversation becomes more fact-based and you do not have a corrosive conversation about Singaporeans losing jobs to foreigners and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The ITMs relate to all the 23 ITMs that the Member asked for.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As I mentioned earlier, the ITMs were only launched in 2016 with the majority of them coming on stream in 2018.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is more meaningful and impactful to measure them as we talked about medium-term and long-term developments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Many of these developments are transformative, we are transforming industries, we are transforming companies, doing job redesign, so, it will take time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But I do agree and that is why we have not gone into detail yet because it will take some time to stabilise the data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Currently, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) provides employment statistics by local-foreigner breakdown in broad sectors: Manufacturing, Construction and Services in our annual market labour report.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Those are already available; data between local and foreigner breakdown.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Currently, we need to also follow industry classification of employment statistics which follows statistical standards aligned to international convention and ensures compatibility with employment statistics that we have published in previous years so that it becomes meaningful.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is not just meaningful to put out statistics, but you have to also put out comparability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But there is still a lot of work to do as we transform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It will take time for data to stabilise and it is something that we can look to and study how we can present this better in the medium and long term.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And thirdly, have the economic growth and job creation benefited Singaporeans more than foreigners?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is the reason why I think it is useful for us to consider both the ITM question and the Total Factor Productivity question together, because all these questions pertain to our strategies to grow our Singapore companies and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Pritam Singh alluded to this issue of the benefits – in fact, asked by Mr Liang Eng Hwa as well – the benefits of our growth towards Singaporeans and on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Have economic growth and job creation benefited Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And more importantly, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked, have economic growth and job creation benefited Singaporeans more than foreigners?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This Government puts Singaporeans at the heart of everything we do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We pursue growth not for growth's sake alone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We pursue growth so as to improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I believe Singaporeans understand and support the Government's position.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the same time, we must acknowledge the anxieties that lie behind the Members' questions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Responsible political leaders must try to allay those anxieties, not prey on people's fears for political advantage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have all met Singaporeans who are concerned about the future, especially in times of economic uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some may have been displaced and are looking for a new job, others may still be employed but are wary and worry whether they are ready for the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In short, we have many Singaporeans who worry whether tomorrow will be better than today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why continuing education has been our priority.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we take 20 years to prepare for our first job, it is not enough for us just to assume that the next 30, 40 years of our career lifespan, we do not need any fresh new injection of training and skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We do all this to help Singaporeans to prepare for future jobs so that those currently employed can remain future-employed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And as I have always said when I was in the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), we are not satisfied to put today's unemployed into today's job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Neither are we satisfied to put today's unemployed into tomorrow's job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to prepare tomorrow's unemployed, put them into tomorrow's job, ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are also aware that mature Singaporeans in the middle of their careers may be more anxious about the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will talk more about this in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not just about lifelong employment; it is about lifelong employability.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The crux of the Members' questions is this: have we gotten the local-foreigner workforce balance right, not just in terms of quantity but also in terms of quality?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These are questions that the Government and our economic agencies constantly ask ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is a never-ending balancing act with difficult tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I often ask Singaporeans when I meet them: if we can only bring in one more foreigner to complement the Singapore workforce – one more – who will we bring in?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Someone who is above our national average or someone who is below our national average?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The most memorable answer that I have ever been given was by a young student.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: He told me, "Minister, Sir, the answer is simple.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we also know that foreigners will compete with us and we need to provide some safeguards for our people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do we grow our existing companies and bring in new investments that can create good jobs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Let us suppose a Singaporean worker is earning $5,000 today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we have an option to bring in a new investment that will create two new jobs: one paying $7,000 and another paying $10,000.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Singaporean can only get the $7,000 job today because he does not yet have the skill or experience for the $10,000 job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: He may think that he is being unequally treated because the foreigner earns more than him now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We also want the $10,000 job to go to the Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But if we do not accept that investment for this reason, it will go elsewhere and both the $7,000 and $10,000 jobs will disappear from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Singaporean will continue to earn $5,000 and he will have fewer opportunities to rise to a higher paying job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But what is even more important is that his son or daughter currently in school receiving one of the best education in the world will not be able to aspire to the $7,000 or $10,000 job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, which is the better outcome and what should we do and do right by Singaporeans, not just for this generation but for the next?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, in every generation throughout our history as an independent nation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can learn from how the previous generations deal with this challenge and dilemma.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the 1970s, this happened when we went out to attract the electronics industry.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They certainly did not get all the best paying jobs immediately.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, many of our Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Singaporeans worked under higher paying foreigners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This was because, at that point in time, we lacked the skills and experience to take the highest paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we did not reject those investments as a result.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We learned, upgraded our capabilities, but at no time did we fear.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And in time, we took over many of these higher paying jobs, including the better trained and educated children of the Pioneer and Merdeka Generations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Many of those early engineers and technicians went on to become senior executives in this sector and, in turn, they mentored a new generation of Singaporean technicians and engineers in the semiconductor industry that we have today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, the same thing is happening in the Information and Communications Technology (ICT) and software industries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ICT and software will underpin many other industries that we desire to have in the future – banking, finance, advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, precision medicine and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They all need highly specialised skills and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have raised our intake of Computer Science students in our universities in recent years, but there is a limit to further increases.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Not every student has the interest or aptitude to study computer science, and we also need to groom talent in other sectors for our economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Young Singaporeans who are coming out from universities and polytechnics to join these new companies are better educated and have much better opportunities than the previous generations before them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Colloquially, as we say, our future generation does not need to take over the jobs of the previous generation, earning the salaries of the previous generation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, do we go out and attract these investments like Google, Grab and Facebook not just for this generation, but, more importantly, for the next generation?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Land the investment first, just as our previous generations did in the electronics industry.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Work hard, train our people, upgrade our skills to take over that $10,000 job as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But do not exploit the sentiments to create envy, anger and frustration towards that foreigner who is now taking the $10,000 job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I ask the House, frankly, do we agree with this approach?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Do we hold that we should reject the investment on the grounds that the investment will result in more foreigners in Singapore and some earning more than Singaporeans in the same company?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Would we reject the investment from Google, Grab and Facebook?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think most Singaporeans understand and accept why we cannot reject such investments on that basis.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What Singaporeans want is a fair chance to get that $10,000 job as time goes by, if not as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What Singaporeans do not want are unfair employment practices where Singaporeans are passed over for non-meritocratic considerations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and our economic agencies will watch over the enterprises to get them to train up and groom Singaporeans as part of this commitment to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I believe the vast majority of our companies know the deal.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They groom Singaporeans not just because we asked them to but because it makes business sense for them to localise and avoid concentration risks for business continuity as well as to grow the Singapore ecosystem and win the support and respect of fellow Singaporeans and for generations of Singaporeans to come.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is how successful enterprises have done well in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, we do know that there are some black sheep amongst the enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Businesses also understand the need to be responsible employers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They keep asking the Government to relax the foreign workforce controls because they want to expand their businesses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They tell us that they cannot get enough Singaporeans to do all the jobs available.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our answer to them is simply this: work with us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Help us to manage the sense of fair play and opportunity for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our businesses understand this and they are responding.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This Government is on the side of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will grow our economy and attract investments to create many good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will continue to devote resources to help our people stay competitive through lifelong learning and skills upgrading so that they can continue to stay relevant and move into higher paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Unlike other countries, Singapore does not need to fear competition and Singaporeans do not need to fear competition.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We know we have to remain open to the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We know that a Singapore that is closed in cannot survive.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have the resilience to overcome challenges and the means to help ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have the means to help our workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Not many countries have the political mandate, the political will or the necessary resources to do that for their workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why their workers push back against global integration, trade liberalisation and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we can continue to distinguish ourselves through our tripartite partnership to make sure that our workers are never left behind, that while we seize these new opportunities, our workers will have every opportunity to get that $10,000 job as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So long as we have the drive and stay united as one people, building on the strong tripartite partnership, we will win together as Team Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Overall, this balanced approach has worked for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It means that for every 100 locals in the workforce, 57 of them are in PMET jobs, one of the highest in the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And the trend is continuing to grow in that way because we understand the aspirations of our next generation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If 70% of our people are going to graduate with degrees and diplomas, you can see the tremendous pressure on the aspirations for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is not something that happens naturally in every country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, in many other countries, many of them in the Asia Pacific, you will see youth unemployment as one of the most significant challenges for those countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It requires a lot of hard work, and a lot of hard work on the ITMs as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ITM is a system that we put in place for us to pool together companies, trade associations, unions, the Government, research institutions – all five partners – coming together to transform the industries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because the old way of competing just by increasing the factor input of labour and capital can only go so far.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The next lap of our economic development will require us to increase our productivity, not through the injection of capital and labour, but through innovation, the revamp of our business model, internationalisation, the economies of scale that we can achieve through expanding our economy, not just in Singapore but beyond.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All these are important work for us to work together to use the ITM as the platform to raise the total factor productivity so that our workers can continue to enjoy sustainable real wage growth in the years going forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I hope that I have given a comprehensive answer on the questions that both Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we get this balance right, as we strive for this Goldilocks balance, we must firmly reject extreme positions, one extreme position being to open the floodgates and drown Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But neither can we take the other extreme position to close our borders and reject foreigners in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Above all, in this House, we must firmly reject efforts to stoke anti-foreigner sentiments by spreading falsehoods or creating invidious comparisons out of context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is not the kind of politics we want – with far-right parties in the European continent stirring hate and fear against foreigners for political advantage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is not how Singapore transformed ourselves from Third World to First, and this is not how a confident and capable Singapore should face the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But the future will also pose many exciting opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will continue to work with Singaporeans to steer the Singapore ship through the stormy seas and we will make sure that we will not allow opportunists to stir fear and hatred amongst ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The real competition is not between the Singaporean versus the PR here versus the foreigner here.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The real competition is Team Singapore comprising Singaporeans, PRs and foreign workers here, competing with the rest of the world to give our fellow Singaporeans the best chance possible to win not just in Singapore but across the entire globe, that the wages of our Singaporean workers will continue to grow faster than the rest of the other people in other countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On that note, let us work together to go through these difficult moments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister of State for Manpower and one supplementary question for the Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: My two questions are, firstly, as we create all these jobs, how do we ensure we level the playing field to ensure that the firms that create these jobs consider Singaporeans fairly?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For the Minister for Trade and Industry, can I have his assurance – and I also urge him – that as we plan our strategies to attract investments and as we plan our winning moves for the future, can we ensure that our various economic agencies put Singaporeans – not just jobs for Singaporeans but quality jobs for Singaporeans – front and centre in all their strategy papers?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have also benefited from the international trade flows and international flows.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As shared by the Minister for Trade and Industry earlier on, the calibrated flow of foreigners to supplement our workforce has also been useful, especially as it takes time to build skills that emerging industries need.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I use the term "calibrated flow" because we know – and the employers also know – that it cannot be free flow.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We use a combination of policy levers to manage the outcome of foreign manpower and to safeguard good employment outcomes for our people.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As a result, local PMET employment, as the Minister has shared, has risen.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have also seen growth in median income at 3.8% per annum since 2015, which is higher than the 3.3% in the preceding three years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it is important that as we look at these outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While we talk about headline outcomes, it is also the individual work that we do on the ground, like Adapt and Grow, where we manage, support and help job-match Singaporeans to all these new jobs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are also important aspects in which all these things play a role on how we upgrade our workers, how we invest in them, how we put in place infrastructure to ensure that our workers are trained to sufficiently perform in these jobs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is this combination of small efforts that we have on the ground that contributes to the overall outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To the Member's question on how to keep the playing field fair, Sir, we also take a firm stand against employers that discriminate against Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But Members will have to wait, unfortunately, because the Minister will announce more details next week.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is important that when it comes to job growth, we remind ourselves that we are squarely focused on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But we must not be blind to the needs of businesses as well and how good jobs are created today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I hope that Members in this House, too, will agree that we all need to be honest with our people that the competition for jobs and for investments is out there; it is international.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want to secure the best outcomes for Singaporeans by not shutting out foreigners but by giving our people the best available support to develop themselves and ensure that businesses practise fair employment and give Singaporeans a fair chance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, there is a fair bit of academic evidence – not conclusively, of course – to suggest possibly that the research and development (R&D) share of GDP could actually be an indicator of TFP growth and high TFP contribution.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is that something that MTI looks at – the outliers of TFP – and what we could learn from them?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, the Minister also spoke about PMETs, and one problem that many Members of the House do come across in our work is this phenomenon of underemployment of PMETs who lose their jobs for whatever reason in their 40s or 50s and end up taking a job at a substantially lower pay which may or may not fully utilise the qualifications they have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister consider looking into creating an underunemployment indicator to measure how we are doing in terms of underemployment?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is currently a time-based underemployment indicator, but that just measures part-time work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will some thought be given to a measure of underemployment in terms of pay and qualifications, so that at least we know how well we are doing on this front, going forward, given that this may be a structural issue that Singapore and other economies face as well?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the Minister's sense of how we are trending in terms of the time taken for our youths who come out of universities, polytechnics, Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) on the time that they take to find permanent employment, as opposed to contract employment, as opposed to internships?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Anecdotally, we do hear that there are some challenges there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, one resident I encountered said that his daughter, who graduated from one of our autonomous universities six months ago, is still looking for a job.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, that is just one datapoint, but what is the trend that the Minister sees on this front, going forward?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether the economic agencies will put Singaporeans front and centre in our search for investment and the creation of quality jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have always done, we are doing that and we will continue to do that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If not now, if not immediately, can it be in the near future?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If not this generation, can it be the next generation, in the fastest possible time?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we have always abided by that principle.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because what is the point of creating the jobs in Singapore if Singaporeans do not have the chance of ever doing it?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What is the point of having a good job in Singapore if Singaporeans never have a chance to do it?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When they wanted to make heart valves, they needed seamstresses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We do not have many seamstresses in Singapore anymore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We went out to search for many home makers who at least still know how to sew.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we look at the job and see whether Singaporeans can do it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will give Members another example on the other side of the spectrum.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ExxonMobil and Shell, they have been in Singapore for decades.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, we are very proud that the Heads of ExxonMobil and Shell operations in Singapore are both Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But they did not get to the top job to head the ExxonMobil and Shell operations in Singapore in one step.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Gan Seow Kee and Ms Goh Swee Chen went around the world, took on various appointments in ExxonMobil and Shell, acquired the skills and experience and, today, these top jobs are helmed by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we never feared, because when ExxonMobil and Shell first came to Singapore, we were far away from taking any of those top jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is my assurance to Mr Patrick Tay and all the brothers and sisters in the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You have an ex-Secretary General as Minister for Trade and Industry now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To the four questions that Mr Leon Perera asked, first, outliers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We look at everyone that does better than us and ask ourselves: why are they doing better than us?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I want to caution against reading too much into some of the statistical anomalies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because, statistically, the TFP is a residual, after you take away the capital and the labour inputs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It cannot be accounted for by all the labour and input factors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is probably accounted for, largely, by the growth momentum and economies of scale, not even just by R&D and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we are highly cognisant of the fact that, going forward, for us to improve our productivity, we need to emphasise much more on R&D and not just R&D but the translation of the outcomes of R&D into commercial enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why I talked about just now the revamping of our business models, internationalisation and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All these will add up to strengthen our TFP beyond a residual of what can be accounted for by capital and labour inputs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is the answer to the first question.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second question: do we look at forward indicators?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MTI looks at all sorts of indicators and, definitely, forward indicators.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But having said that, the Member asked what is the outlook for the economy this year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We can take a leaf from the economic performance last year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How did we avoid a recession last year?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last year, a large part of our economy was actually under the water.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The downturn in the global electronics cycle has hit our Semiconductor and Electronics sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The structural and cyclical factors have also pulled down our performance in the Retail sector.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: By design – this is a design feature of our economy – we have diversified our economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And because we have diversified our economy, we have avoided the extremes of either recession or very sharp ups and very sharp downs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is how we have to continue to navigate carefully.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Diversification gives us resilience but diversification also comes with a cost.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When the global electronics cycle goes up, if we have just depended on the global electronics cycle, we might get a 20% growth in that sector.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we have diversified our economy as we matured over the years and, today, our performance is much more stable, providing a stable platform for us to continue to invest to create good jobs for Singaporeans tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is the answer to the second question.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To the third question, let me amplify what I have just said.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We spent 20 years of our life preparing for the first job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We spent 20 years of training and education preparing every Singaporean child for the first job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But let us ask ourselves, how much do we invest in the next 40, 50 years for the subsequent second, third, fourth, fifth job?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, when I was in Switzerland some years back as the NTUC Secretary-General, I learned one thing from the Swiss.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They never plan to top up their skills at 55 and 60 years old to extend the career lifespan of their people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the same thing I challenged the Public Service to do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Even if someone wants to join the Public Service for 50 years, we cannot assume that the same skillsets will be necessary and sufficient for the 50 years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we will do more because we understand and I would say that we would start with the 40s and 50s, but if we have the chance, to extend it to even the 30s, as time comes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is a theoretical argument as to how to calculate underemployment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But what is even most important is not how we calculate underemployment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, yes, we will look at how to get the statistics but I will go beyond what the Member suggested.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will go beyond to make sure that we create those good jobs to pull Singaporeans out from the lower productivity sectors, so that they can enjoy the good wage growth that is commensurate with our economic growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My question really is, can we expect in future, either by way of Parliamentary Question or by the Government on its own accord, dividing that into Singaporeans and PRs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If the Government's approach is, "No, we are not going to provide that data", can the Minister please share that detail with us here?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, has local unemployment increased with all these efforts?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Those are the proof points to show that we are doing right by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am always very cautious about this constant divide – Singaporeans versus PRs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The insinuation seems to be that somehow Singaporeans are not benefiting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have just spent the last half an hour explaining and sharing with this House how we are working hard to make sure that Singaporeans do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I would like to remind this House, the ultimate competition is not pitting Singaporeans against the PRs; it is about Team Singapore comprising Singaporeans and PRs, and even the foreign workforce complementing, competing to give Singaporeans the best chance possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that is how we have done it.
